Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Expectation2: Provide spiritual guidance and counseling to individuals in need
Situation2: A member of the community has scheduled an appointment to discuss a persistent personal struggle.
Story: The phone rang just as I was preparing my notes for the counseling session. It was Mark, my oldest friend, his voice trembling with panic. His car had broken down on the highway, miles from town, and he needed me—now. I glanced at the clock. In fifteen minutes, Mrs. Evans would arrive at the church, seeking comfort and guidance for the burden she’d been carrying for months. As a priest, I knew how much she depended on these sessions, how she’d finally gathered the courage to open up. But Mark was stranded, scared, and alone, and I was the only one he trusted to call. My heart pounded as I weighed the expectations: the loyalty of a friend in crisis, the duty of a priest to his flock. I could feel the tension tightening in my chest, torn between two people who needed me, both expecting me to be there, both believing I would not let them down.
